practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a characteristic of an entrepreneur named in the specification?
A) Shyness
B) Risk taking
C) Avoiding decisions
D) Ignoring customers
practice_questions.marks:
B) Risk taking [1 mark]
The four named characteristics are creativity, risk taking, determination and confidence. A, C and D are the opposite of what entrepreneurs need. Attempt every MCQ — blank answers score zero.

practice_questions.text: Identify one non-financial reward an entrepreneur might gain from setting up their own business.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of: independence / being their own boss; personal satisfaction; the chance to solve a problem they care about; flexibility over hours; building something lasting; creative freedom. [1 mark]
Do not accept ‘profit’ or any purely financial answer — the question specifies non-financial.

practice_questions.text: Outline one risk an entrepreneur takes when starting a new business. (Context: Aisha is leaving her job as a salaried graphic designer to set up her own freelance branding studio in Manchester, using £12,000 of personal savings as start-up capital.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a relevant risk (e.g. losing her savings, losing her guaranteed salary, unlimited liability).
2 marks: adds development with application to Aisha — e.g. ‘Aisha is giving up her guaranteed designer salary (1), so if client work is slow in the first few months she will have no regular income and may need to use the £12,000 savings to cover her rent (1).’
A single-word answer (e.g. ‘money’) scores 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way creativity helps an entrepreneur to develop a successful business idea. (Context: Sir James Dyson designed the world’s first bagless vacuum cleaner after noticing his own vacuum losing suction.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies creativity as seeing a problem others miss (AO1).
2 marks: applies creativity to the Dyson example (AO2) — e.g. noticing the suction issue in his own home.
3 marks: develops the consequence for the business — the cyclone solved a widespread customer problem, giving Dyson a genuinely new product with no direct rival.
Indicative answer: ‘Creativity allows an entrepreneur to spot a problem that rivals have ignored (1). Sir James Dyson noticed his own vacuum losing suction and invented the bagless cyclone as a solution (2), which gave him a genuinely different product and a gap in the market with no direct rival (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how risk and reward might influence the decision of an entrepreneur to leave their job and start their own business. (Context: Dan, 28, earns £32,000 as a head chef. He is considering leaving to open his own street-food burger van using £18,000 of personal savings.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning anchored to Dan’s case. Chain 1 (risk): giving up £32,000 salary + using £18,000 savings → unlimited liability as a sole trader → personal assets exposed if the van fails → specific consequence (e.g. Dan could lose his whole savings cushion and struggle to pay rent). Chain 2 (reward): independence / full profits / doing work he loves → potential for higher earnings than salary if the van succeeds → ability to grow the idea into a second van. Sustained application to Dan.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear application to Dan at key steps, reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but not fully linked to Dan; some context used but generic in places.
Emerging: Lists risks and rewards abstractly without applying them to the case study. A generic answer with no application to Dan cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether the rewards of starting a new business always outweigh the risks for a first-time entrepreneur. (Context: two recent university graduates in Leeds are choosing between (A) accepting graduate jobs paying £28,000 each or (B) pooling their £10,000 combined savings to launch a subscription fresh-juice delivery service.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument developing both sides with reference to the graduates’ specific circumstances (small savings, no business track record, two graduate jobs foregone). Reaches a supported judgement that weighs one side more heavily, or says ‘it depends on X’ with X justified (e.g. depends on whether they can keep one graduate salary as a safety net).
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear judgement, some application to the graduates.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, judgement restates earlier points without weighting.
Emerging: One-sided argument, no judgement, or no application to the case.

Arguments that rewards outweigh risks: independence, potential upside of a successful start-up (Gymshark valuation), early-career years are the easiest time to take risk (no mortgage, no children).
Arguments that risks outweigh rewards: giving up £56,000 combined graduate salary, only £10,000 capital is thin, unlimited liability as sole traders / partners, high early-stage failure rate, no business experience.
Strong judgements note that launching while one graduate keeps a salary, or trialling the subscription part-time before quitting, would cut the risk without killing the reward. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: Which production method is most suitable for making one-off bespoke wedding cakes?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Selects 'Job production'.
Secure: Selects 'Job production'.
Developing: Selects a plausible distractor (e.g. batch).
Emerging: Selects an unrelated option.
Mark allocation: Job production = 1 mark; any other = 0.

practice_questions.text: Identify one form of production technology named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Names automation, computers or robotics.
Developing / Emerging (0): Vague term ('machinery') or off-spec answer such as 'the internet'.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason a bakery such as Warburtons uses batch production rather than flow production. (Context: Warburtons produces many different bread varieties each day from the same factory.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): A valid reason (e.g. allows the same line to make different breads) + brief development tied to the bakery (e.g. so both white and wholemeal loaves can come from one ovens by cleaning between batches).
Secure (2): Reason + development.
Developing (1): Reason only, no development, or development lacks application.
Emerging (0): Incorrect or missing reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit for a car manufacturer of using robotics on the assembly line. (Context: Nissan's Sunderland plant builds over 300,000 cars a year and uses hundreds of robotic arms for welding and painting.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Correct benefit (e.g. consistent quality) + development (robots perform the same weld identically every time) + application to Nissan (across 300,000 vehicles a year this removes fault variation that customers would notice).
Secure (3): Benefit + development + application.
Developing (2): Benefit + one development or application but not both.
Emerging (1): Benefit named only, or question restated.
0: No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK bakery of switching from batch production to flow production. (Context: a medium-sized UK bakery currently batch-produces 20 bread varieties; it is considering a flow line dedicated to its best-selling white sliced loaf.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two developed chains of reasoning, each anchored in the bakery context. For example: lower unit cost because the oven runs continuously without changeover, which enables a lower retail price and higher market share; reduced flexibility because the flow line cannot switch to other varieties, which means any drop in white-loaf demand cannot be absorbed elsewhere.
Secure (4-5): Two strands of analysis, application sustained throughout.
Developing (2-3): Generic points; application weak or only once.
Emerging (1-2): List of factors with no chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a UK car manufacturer should invest £200 million in new robotic assembly technology. (Context: the investment would cut unit costs by 12% but result in around 300 redundancies at a plant employing 4,500 people.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9): Both sides weighed in depth with application (unit cost fall of 12% converted into the lower price or higher margin; 300 of 4,500 jobs put in context of community impact). Supported judgement reached with new evaluative weighting (e.g. depends on how quickly rivals also automate).
Secure (6-7): Both sides, application throughout, judgement made but lightly developed.
Developing (4-5): Both sides treated but as mirror-image lists; judgement missing or unsupported.
Emerging (1-3): One side only, or no use of the scenario numbers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a named purpose of planning business activity?
A) Increasing competition
B) Reducing risk
C) Lowering customer satisfaction
D) Avoiding profit
practice_questions.marks:
B) Reducing risk [1 mark]
The specification names two purposes of planning business activity: reducing risk and helping a business to succeed. Options A, C and D are the opposite of what planning aims to achieve.

practice_questions.text: State one role of a business plan.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of: identifying markets; helping to obtain finance; identifying resources the business needs to operate; achieving aims and objectives. [1 mark]
Do not accept vague answers such as ‘it helps the business’ — the role must be named from the specification list.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason why a lender might ask to see a business plan before approving a loan. (Context: Maria is asking her high-street bank for a £25,000 loan to open a small bakery in Sheffield.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a relevant reason (e.g. to check the business can repay; to see the forecast sales; to check there is real market demand).
2 marks: adds development with application to Maria — e.g. ‘The bank will want to see Maria’s cash flow forecast (1), so it can judge whether the bakery can generate enough monthly income to cover the £25,000 loan repayments without running out of cash (1).’
Bare-term answers (e.g. ‘safety’) score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a business plan can help a new business to identify the resources it needs. (Context: Dan is writing a plan to launch a mobile coffee van at Leeds festivals and weekend markets.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies that the plan lists the resources required (AO1).
2 marks: applies to Dan’s van — e.g. coffee machine, the van itself, cups, coffee beans, a generator, insurance, a stall pitch fee (AO2).
3 marks: develops the consequence — listing the resources lets Dan add up the start-up cost and see whether his savings will cover it, or whether he needs a loan.
Indicative answer: ‘A business plan asks the founder to list every resource needed to operate (1). For Dan this means the van, the espresso machine, coffee beans, cups, a generator and festival pitch fees (2), which he can then price to see whether his savings cover the start-up cost or whether he needs a bank loan before launch (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how writing a business plan can help a new entrepreneur to reduce the risk of failure. (Context: Leah is preparing to leave her office job to open an independent bookshop in Bristol. She has £22,000 in savings and is writing her first business plan.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning anchored to Leah. Chain 1: the plan forces market research → Leah confirms the catchment around her chosen Bristol street contains enough readers → reduces the risk of opening in the wrong location → named consequence (e.g. avoids signing a lease that sales cannot support). Chain 2: the plan forces a cash flow forecast → Leah sees that month 2 is her tightest month → arranges an overdraft in advance → protects her £22,000 savings from being wiped out by one bad month.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear application to Leah at key steps, at least one reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but loose application to Leah.
Emerging: Lists ways a plan reduces risk abstractly without applying them to the bookshop. A generic answer with no application cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether writing a detailed business plan is always worth the effort for a first-time entrepreneur. (Context: Ade is planning to launch an online tutoring service from his bedroom. He has two weeks before term starts and is choosing between spending that time writing a 25-page plan or spending it on building the website and finding his first five clients.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument developing both sides, applied to Ade’s decision, with a supported judgement that either weights one side (e.g. ‘a lighter plan is enough when start-up capital is small’) or makes an explicit recommendation with evaluative comment.
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear judgement, some application to Ade.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, judgement restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported argument.

Arguments that a detailed plan IS worth it: forces market research, identifies resources, is required if Ade later needs finance, flushes out hidden costs (website hosting, DBS check, marketing), provides a yardstick for measuring his own progress.
Arguments against a detailed 25-page plan for Ade: his start-up cost is tiny so he does not need a bank loan, the market changes weekly during exam season, time spent writing is time not spent winning clients, forecasts for online tutoring are unreliable with no past sales data, a one-page plan may be enough.
Supported judgement: for Ade, a short written plan is valuable; a full 25-page document is not, because the risk reduction does not outweigh the opportunity cost of losing two weeks of client acquisition. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: Which of the following best describes quality assurance?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Selects 'Building quality checks into every stage of the process so defects are prevented.'
Developing / Emerging (0): Selects a plausible distractor such as an end-of-line inspection (which describes quality control).

practice_questions.text: State one impact on a business of a product recall.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Names a valid impact — damage to reputation, lost sales, fines, cost of replacing the product, lost customer trust.
Developing / Emerging (0): Vague response ('bad'), or confuses recall with refund.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason quality is important for a UK supermarket selling fresh food. (Context: a national supermarket chain competes against discount rivals on both price and food safety.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Valid reason (e.g. to protect reputation) + development tied to the supermarket (e.g. so customers continue to trust the fresh-food aisle over discount rivals).
Secure (2): Reason + development.
Developing (1): Reason only, or development lacks application.
Emerging (0): Incorrect or missing reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a car manufacturer of using quality assurance rather than quality control. (Context: a UK car plant builds 300,000 vehicles a year; each defective car door costs £280 in wasted parts and labour if rejected at the end of the line.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Correct benefit (fewer defects make it through to the finished car) + development (faults are spotted and fixed earlier in the line) + application (prevents £280 of wasted parts and labour on each of many defective doors across 300,000 vehicles).
Secure (3): Benefit + development + application.
Developing (2): Benefit + development or application but not both.
Emerging (1): Benefit named only.
0: No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK food manufacturer of failing to maintain quality standards. (Context: a medium-sized ready-meal manufacturer supplies three major supermarkets; a 2% rise in customer complaints last quarter triggered one retailer to review its contract.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two developed chains of reasoning, each anchored in the scenario. For example: reputational damage — complaints rise, supermarket reviews the contract, potential loss of a major buyer with large revenue; financial cost — higher returns and recalls reduce profit margin as faulty stock must be replaced at the manufacturer's expense.
Secure (4-5): Two strands, application sustained throughout.
Developing (2-3): Generic points, application weak or only once.
Emerging (1-2): List of factors, no chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a small UK bakery should invest £15,000 in a quality assurance training programme for its staff. (Context: the bakery currently uses end-of-line quality control; it scraps around £200 of bread each week due to late-stage defects and has received a poor online review about burnt loaves.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9): Balanced discussion of the case for assurance (lower scrap cost, better reputation) and against (high upfront cost of training, small size may not justify investment). Supported judgement reached: recommendation clearly stated, justified by a named weighting factor (e.g. the £200 weekly scrap and reputational damage outweigh a one-off £15,000 cost). Application is sustained to the bakery.
Secure (6-7): Both sides weighed, recommendation made but evaluation less developed.
Developing (4-5): Both sides listed but as mirror-image lists; judgement weak or missing.
Emerging (1-3): One side only or no meaningful engagement with the £15,000 / £200 data.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is an example of e-commerce?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Selects 'A customer ordering a dress from the ASOS website.'
Developing / Emerging (0): Selects a face-to-face or telesales distractor.

practice_questions.text: Identify one method of selling named on the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): E-commerce, face to face, or telesales.
Developing / Emerging (0): Vague term ('marketing') or non-spec answer.

practice_questions.text: Outline one benefit to a customer of a shop offering good product knowledge. (Context: a UK bike shop selling a wide range of road, mountain and children's bikes.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Valid benefit (e.g. buys the right bike first time) + development applied to the bike shop (e.g. a knowledgeable member of staff explains gear and frame differences so a first-time buyer does not return it).
Secure (2): Benefit + development.
Developing (1): Benefit only or weak application.
Emerging (0): Incorrect or missing benefit.

practice_questions.text: A small online clothing retailer makes 1,200 sales in its first month at an average price of £32. Calculate the total sales revenue.
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: £38,400. Mark allocation: 1 mark for correct method (1,200 × £32), 1 mark for correct answer. Correct working earns the method mark even if the final answer is wrong. Must show £ sign and show working for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way e-commerce has influenced the activity of a UK high-street retailer. (Context: a national clothing retailer has closed 30 of its 210 high-street shops in the last two years while opening a new online fulfilment centre.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Valid influence (e.g. shifted costs from rent to fulfilment) + development (customers increasingly prefer browsing and ordering online) + application (closing 30 shops and opening an online fulfilment centre moves fixed costs out of prime rents).
Secure (3): Influence + development + application.
Developing (2): Influence + development or application.
Emerging (1): Influence named only.
0: No valid influence.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact of good customer service on a UK food retailer competing against discount supermarkets. (Context: a mid-sized UK food retailer competes with Aldi and Lidl on price and with Waitrose on service; it has just launched a staff training programme in product knowledge.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two developed strands of reasoning anchored in the scenario. For example: better product knowledge builds trust, which helps retain shoppers who might otherwise drift to cheaper rivals; engaged staff encourage higher average basket size because customers are guided to higher-margin items. Application to the mid-sized retailer is sustained.
Secure (4-5): Two strands, application throughout.
Developing (2-3): Generic analysis; application weak.
Emerging (1-2): List of points, no chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following business structures has unlimited liability?
A) Private limited company (Ltd)
B) Public limited company (Plc)
C) Sole trader
D) A company with a Royal Charter
practice_questions.marks:
C) Sole trader [1 mark]
Sole traders and partnerships have unlimited liability. Ltd and Plc shareholders have limited liability. Attempt every MCQ — blank answers score zero.

practice_questions.text: Identify one feature of a public limited company (Plc).
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of: shares can be sold to the general public on the stock exchange; shareholders have limited liability; a separate legal entity from its owners; must publish annual accounts; can raise large sums of finance through share issues. [1 mark]
Loose paraphrases that miss the Plc-specific point (e.g. ‘sells shares’ — so does an Ltd) score 0.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason a small business might choose to operate as a partnership rather than a sole trader. (Context: Aisha and Hannah have both qualified as architects and are considering setting up together in Bristol.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a relevant reason (e.g. shared skills, shared workload, more start-up finance between two owners).
2 marks: adds development with application to Aisha and Hannah — e.g. ‘A partnership lets Aisha and Hannah combine their design and project management skills (1), meaning the new practice can take on larger projects from day one than either could manage alone (1).’
Bare-term answers (e.g. ‘money’) score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of operating as a private limited company (Ltd) rather than as a sole trader. (Context: Marcus runs a kitchen refurbishment business in Newcastle and is considering incorporating.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies an advantage (e.g. limited liability, ability to raise more finance, separate legal status) (AO1).
2 marks: applies to Marcus — e.g. if a customer sues over a faulty installation, only the company’s assets are at risk (AO2).
3 marks: develops the consequence — Marcus’s home and personal savings are protected, which makes larger-scale contracts less risky to accept.
Indicative answer: ‘As an Ltd, Marcus would benefit from limited liability (1). If a customer sued the business over a faulty kitchen installation, only the company’s assets would be at risk (2), so Marcus could bid on larger contracts without exposing his home and personal savings to claims if something went wrong (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse one benefit and one drawback of a private limited company (Ltd) floating on the stock exchange to become a public limited company (Plc). (Context: DrumBeat Ltd is a Manchester-based headphone brand turning over £18m a year. Its founders are considering an Initial Public Offering to fund international expansion.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains anchored to DrumBeat. Benefit chain: flotation raises large-scale finance → DrumBeat can fund the US warehouses and marketing spend it cannot fund as an Ltd → speeds up international growth → protects against rivals entering first. Drawback chain: selling shares to the public dilutes founder control → DrumBeat’s founders no longer decide strategy alone → must justify every quarter to shareholders → risk of short-term pressure on long-term design investment.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear application to DrumBeat, reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but generic in places, limited application.
Emerging: Lists benefits and drawbacks without applying them. A generic answer with no context cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Recommend whether Leo should operate as a sole trader or a private limited company (Ltd) when launching his new cycle-courier business. Justify your recommendation. (Context: Leo is leaving his salaried office job to run a one-person bicycle courier service in central Cambridge. He expects to earn around £28,000 in year one and will be carrying high-value parcels for law firms.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument developing both options, applied to Leo, with a clear recommendation that weights one side. The judgement introduces a new weighting rather than restating both sides — e.g. ‘the value of the parcels tips the balance towards Ltd status even though set-up is simpler as a sole trader.’
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear recommendation, some application to Leo.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, recommendation restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported recommendation.

Arguments for sole trader: free and simple to set up, no filing at Companies House, keeps all profit, year-one turnover of £28,000 is low so the administrative cost of an Ltd is hard to justify.
Arguments for Ltd: high-value parcels mean high liability if something is lost or damaged; as a sole trader, Leo’s own assets (home, savings) are at risk; Ltd status protects personal assets via limited liability; also easier to take on corporate clients who prefer dealing with companies.
Supported recommendation: Ltd status — the unusual feature of carrying high-value legal parcels creates a liability exposure that outweighs the admin cost of incorporation. A sole trader would be the simpler and cheaper option for a low-value courier; it is not the right call here. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the MOST likely main objective of a brand-new start-up in its first year?
A) International expansion
B) Survival
C) Taking over rivals
D) Maximising shareholder dividends
practice_questions.marks:
B) Survival [1 mark]
In the first year, costs are high, revenue is unstable and the priority is covering monthly bills. Growth, takeovers and dividends come later. Attempt every MCQ — blank answers score zero.

practice_questions.text: Identify one business objective other than profit.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of: survival, growth, providing a service, market share. [1 mark]
Do not accept ‘make money’ or any wording that is just a restatement of profit.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason why a business’s objectives might change as it grows. (Context: Helm Cycles started as a one-person bicycle repair shop in Bristol in 2023. It now employs six staff and is opening a second shop.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a relevant reason (e.g. the business is past the fragile early phase; it now has resources to grow; competition has changed).
2 marks: adds development with application to Helm Cycles — e.g. ‘Helm Cycles is no longer fighting for survival (1), so it can shift its main objective from covering monthly costs to growth by opening a second shop (1).’
Bare-term answers (e.g. ‘money’) score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a charity might set providing a service as its main objective rather than profit. (Context: a small UK charity in Manchester runs a food bank for families on low incomes.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies that charities exist to serve a cause, not to generate profit for owners (AO1).
2 marks: applies to the Manchester food bank — e.g. its purpose is to supply food to struggling families, not to earn surplus cash (AO2).
3 marks: develops the consequence — a profit objective would conflict with the charity’s mission, while a service objective measures what success looks like (number of families fed).
Indicative answer: ‘Charities exist to serve a social cause rather than to earn profit for owners (1). For the Manchester food bank, that cause is supplying food to struggling families (2), so a service objective — measured by the number of families fed each week — tracks what success actually looks like, whereas a profit objective would conflict with the charity’s reason for existing (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse one reason why different businesses set different objectives. (Context: compare a UK start-up food truck in its first year with a Plc like Unilever operating in 190 countries.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning anchored to the two contrasting businesses. Chain 1 (start-up): thin cash reserves / first-year uncertainty → survival becomes the main objective → decisions focused on covering monthly costs → named consequence (e.g. the food truck prioritises low rent and a simple menu to protect cash). Chain 2 (Unilever): established market position and deep cash reserves → survival is no longer at stake → focus shifts to growth and market share in 190 countries → named consequence (e.g. Unilever spends heavily on new product launches and acquisitions).
Secure: Two developed chains, clear contrast, at least one reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but generic.
Emerging: Lists objectives without linking them to the different business contexts. A generic answer cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether profit should always be the most important objective for a UK private limited company. (Context: FairBean Ltd is a family-owned fair-trade coffee importer in Leeds with 15 staff. The founders have always said their aim is to give Colombian farmers a better price than the big brands, even when this means smaller profits for the business.)
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument developing both sides with reference to FairBean, reaching a supported judgement that weights one side (e.g. ‘for FairBean, service to farmers can be the main objective because the founders chose this model; for a Plc answerable to thousands of shareholders the answer differs’). Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear judgement, some application to FairBean. Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, judgement restates earlier points without weighting. Emerging: One-sided argument, no judgement, or no application. Arguments for profit as main objective: profit funds wages, reinvestment, survival and future expansion; without profit the business eventually folds and cannot help anyone. Arguments against profit as main objective: FairBean’s purpose is the fair-trade mission; a service objective is consistent with that mission and is what customers pay a premium for; prioritising short-term profit could undermine the brand’s credibility and drive away ethical consumers. Supported judgement: profit is necessary but not sufficient for FairBean; the right framing is probably that profit is a constraint (must stay in the black) but service to farmers remains the lead objective. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is one of the three tests that consumer law applies to products?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Selects 'Fit for purpose' (or equivalent: satisfactory quality, as described).
Developing / Emerging (0): Selects a non-specification distractor.

practice_questions.text: State one way consumer law can impact a business's reputation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Names a valid impact — e.g. negative publicity, loss of customer trust, damage from a recall, Trading Standards investigation.
Developing / Emerging (0): Vague response ('bad') or off-spec answer.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason a UK retailer might choose to offer free returns that go beyond the legal minimum. (Context: an online clothing retailer offers free next-day returns on every order.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Valid reason (e.g. customers are more confident to order) + development applied to the retailer (e.g. knowing they can return for free, more shoppers click 'buy' for clothes they are unsure about).
Secure (2): Reason + development.
Developing (1): Reason only or weak application.
Emerging (0): Incorrect or missing reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain one impact of a product recall on a UK electronics manufacturer. (Context: the firm has recalled 50,000 tablets after reports that batteries overheat; recalls and replacements are expected to cost around £8 million.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Valid impact (e.g. large direct financial cost plus reputational damage) + development (refunds, shipping and replacement units are expensive to process) + application (£8 million of direct cost on top of lost future sales from a damaged brand).
Secure (3): Impact + development + application.
Developing (2): Impact + development or application.
Emerging (1): Impact named only.
0: No valid impact.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK food manufacturer of breaching the ‘as described’ requirement of consumer law. (Context: the manufacturer labels a ready meal as vegetarian; a test finds trace amounts of meat and supermarkets remove the product from shelves.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two developed strands anchored in the scenario. For example: loss of retailer contracts as supermarkets drop the product, leading to a significant revenue fall; reputational damage among vegetarian customers spreads online and reduces future repeat orders. Application sustained to the food manufacturer.
Secure (4-5): Two strands, application throughout.
Developing (2-3): Generic points, application weak.
Emerging (1-2): Listed points, no chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a small UK online retailer should invest £25,000 in new quality checks and clearer product descriptions to reduce consumer law complaints. (Context: the retailer processed £2.1 million of sales last year and paid out £38,000 in refunds for items that did not match their online description.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9): Both sides weighed with application. For: the £38,000 refund bill and reputational damage already exceed the £25,000 investment, so the change should pay for itself. Against: £25,000 is meaningful for a small retailer, and returns may not fall by enough to cover the cost. Supported judgement (e.g. invest in the change because ongoing refund costs are larger than the one-off spend).
Secure (6-7): Both sides, application, judgement made but less developed.
Developing (4-5): Both sides listed as mirror images, judgement weak or missing.
Emerging (1-3): One side only or no use of the scenario numbers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an external stakeholder?
A) An employee of the business
B) A customer
C) A manager
D) An owner
practice_questions.marks:
B) A customer [1 mark]
External stakeholders sit outside the business. Customers, suppliers, the local community and the government are external. Employees, managers and owners are internal. Attempt every MCQ — blank answers score zero.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which the government is a stakeholder in a UK business.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: collects corporation tax / VAT / income tax / employer National Insurance from the business; regulates business activity through consumer, employment or environmental law; funds public services that healthy businesses support; is affected by unemployment when businesses close. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way a decision to close a local factory might affect the local community. (Context: a food-processing firm in a small Cumbrian town announces it will shut its main factory, which employs 180 local people.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a relevant effect (e.g. unemployment rises, local spending falls, nearby shops lose customers, house prices drop).
2 marks: adds development with application to the Cumbrian town — e.g. ‘180 local people will lose their jobs (1), cutting household spending at local shops and pubs and lowering the whole town’s economic activity (1).’
One-word answers score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way customers can influence the decisions of a business they disapprove of. (Context: in 2020 newspaper reports linked the fast-fashion retailer Boohoo to underpaid garment workers in Leicester.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies that customers can switch away or boycott (AO1).
2 marks: applies to Boohoo — e.g. shoppers stopping purchases after the news (AO2).
3 marks: develops the consequence — the share price fell by 46% in days, and the business had to publicly investigate its supply chain to win customers back.
Indicative answer: ‘Customers can influence a business by choosing to spend their money elsewhere (1). When news stories linked Boohoo to underpaid workers in Leicester, many shoppers switched to rivals (2), cutting 46% off Boohoo’s share price in days, which forced the business to publicly investigate its supply chain to regain customer trust (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how stakeholder conflict might arise when a UK business decides to switch to 24-hour operations. (Context: RapidParcel, a logistics firm based near a residential area in Birmingham, is planning to move to round-the-clock lorry movements from its depot.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning anchored to RapidParcel. Chain 1: owners and customers benefit from 24-hour operations → higher revenue, faster delivery service → profits and service objective both supported. Chain 2: local community (external) and some employees (internal) lose → 3am lorry noise disturbs residents → planning objections or council restrictions → named consequence for RapidParcel (e.g. council tightens operating hours, forcing the firm to run a partial service overnight). Shows the two-way effect.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear application to RapidParcel, at least one reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but loosely applied.
Emerging: Lists stakeholders without building a chain, no application to the case. A generic answer cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Recommend one action a business could take to manage stakeholder conflict when opening a new facility in a residential area. Justify your recommendation. (Context: SunBake Ltd is planning a new bakery on the edge of a quiet residential village in Kent. It will employ 40 people but will need 4am flour deliveries.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument that considers multiple stakeholder groups (local community, employees, owners, council/government), applied to SunBake, with a clear recommendation that weights the most important factor. Examples of recommended actions: investing in quieter delivery vehicles; shifting delivery to 6am; holding a community consultation; hiring locally; sponsoring local amenities.
Secure: Developed arguments, clear recommendation, some application to SunBake.
Developing: Some points made, limited development, recommendation restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported recommendation.

Key tensions to weigh: local community vs owners (noise vs profit); employees (welcome the jobs) vs community (unwelcome disruption); council as regulator (planning permission depends on community satisfaction).
Supported recommendation: a strong answer identifies that community goodwill is critical because SunBake needs the council’s planning permission AND local staff AND local customers — so measures that directly address community concerns (later delivery time, quieter vehicles, visible community investment) outweigh pure profit maximisation in the opening months. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four named location factors on the specification?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Selects 'Level of competition' (or similarly off-spec option).
Developing / Emerging (0): Selects one of the four valid factors (costs, proximity to market, labour, materials).

practice_questions.text: State one factor that influences where a UK business chooses to locate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering / Secure (1): Names costs, proximity to market, labour, or materials.
Developing / Emerging (0): Vague ('the best place') or off-spec answer.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason a UK fish processing business would choose to locate near a fishing port. (Context: the business processes fresh cod and haddock into ready-to-cook fillets for supermarkets.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Valid reason (e.g. proximity to raw materials) + development (e.g. fresh fish is bulky and spoils quickly, so short transport cuts waste and cost).
Secure (2): Reason + development.
Developing (1): Reason only or weak application.
Emerging (0): Incorrect or missing reason.

practice_questions.text: A UK coffee chain is choosing between two shop locations. Location A costs £4,200 in monthly rent and is expected to serve 320 customers per day; location B costs £1,800 in monthly rent and is expected to serve 110 customers per day. Calculate the rent cost per expected daily customer for each location (to the nearest penny) and state which location has the lower rent cost per customer. Assume 30 days of trading per month.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark allocation (4 marks total):
1 mark — Location A daily rent calculation: £4,200 ÷ 30 = £140 per day.
1 mark — Location A rent per customer: £140 ÷ 320 = £0.4375 ≈ £0.44.
1 mark — Location B rent per customer: (£1,800 ÷ 30) ÷ 110 = £60 ÷ 110 = £0.5454 ≈ £0.55.
1 mark — Correct conclusion: Location A has the lower rent cost per customer (£0.44 vs £0.55).
Mastering: Full working shown, final figures to the nearest penny, clear conclusion.
Secure: All four marks won with correct working.
Developing: One or two calculation steps correct but final conclusion wrong or missing.
Emerging: Attempts the calculation but makes multiple errors.
Correct method earns method marks even when a final figure is wrong (e.g. if daily rent calculated correctly but divided by the wrong customer number).

practice_questions.text: Explain one way location can affect the cost base of a UK warehouse operator. (Context: an online retailer is deciding between warehouse sites in Rugby and central London; the Rugby site has rent 60% lower than the London site.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Valid point (location changes fixed costs per unit sold) + development (rent and rates are a large fixed cost; regional sites are cheaper than the capital) + application (60% lower rent in Rugby releases cash the retailer can spend on delivery or pricing).
Secure (3): Point + development + application.
Developing (2): Point + development or application.
Emerging (1): Point named only.
0: No valid point.

practice_questions.text: Recommend whether a growing UK bakery should open its next outlet on a busy high street or in a cheaper out-of-town retail park. (Context: the bakery has £120,000 retained profit to invest, sells mostly to lunchtime office workers, and its five existing shops all sit on busy high streets.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9): Balanced discussion with sustained application. For high street: proximity to target market (lunchtime office workers) supports higher sales; existing five-shop estate proves the model works on a high street. For retail park: lower rent improves margin; free parking could widen the target market. Clear recommendation tied to a named weighting factor (e.g. recommend the high street because the bakery's proven customer profile is office workers, not drivers, so footfall dominates cost savings).
Secure (6-7): Both sides weighed, recommendation made, application present but less developed.
Developing (4-5): Both sides listed as mirror images, no clear recommendation.
Emerging (1-3): One side only or fails to use the scenario (£120,000, five shops, lunchtime office workers).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the first step in the procurement process?
A) Choosing a supplier
B) Receiving the delivery
C) Identifying the goods and services to buy
D) Placing the order
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for selecting option C (Identifying the goods and services to buy). No marks for any other answer.

practice_questions.text: Identify one factor, other than price, that a business might consider when choosing a supplier.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one correct factor: quality, reliability, delivery speed, payment terms, location, ethical practices, or reputation. Precise term required.

practice_questions.text: Outline one way that a short supply chain can benefit a small UK bakery.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid benefit (fresher ingredients / quicker delivery / easier to monitor / lower transport costs / supports local economy). 1 mark for brief development linking the benefit to the bakery context. Mastering: precise benefit with clear linked development. Secure: valid benefit with some development. Developing: benefit stated without clear development. Emerging: vague or partial point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Nissan’s UK car plant might use multiple suppliers for its components rather than relying on a single supplier.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid reason (reduces risk of supply disruption / creates competition among suppliers / prevents over-dependence). 1 mark for applying to Nissan’s context (large-scale assembly / thousands of components / chip shortage exposure). 1 mark for developed explanation (e.g. ‘so that if one supplier fails, production can continue from the other’). Mastering: developed chain tied to context. Secure: reason with application. Developing: reason with limited application. Emerging: reason stated only.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the 2021-22 global semiconductor shortage affected UK car manufacturers such as Nissan.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: shortage of chips → paused or reduced production → lower revenue; backlog of customer orders → damaged reputation / lost sales to competitors; higher costs as firms pay more for scarce components → squeezed profit margins; longer-term move to build more UK or EU supply → higher ongoing costs but reduced future risk. Mastering (5-6): developed chain of reasoning linking cause to business consequence to second-order impact, with specific Nissan application. Secure (3-4): clear reasoning with some application. Developing (2): partial reasoning, limited application. Emerging (1): identifies an effect without chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a small UK bakery should use a single local flour supplier or multiple suppliers.
practice_questions.marks: Candidates should weigh both sides. Single supplier: stronger relationship, bigger bulk discount, simpler ordering, trust on quality — BUT vulnerable if the supplier fails, less competition on price. Multiple suppliers: spreads risk of disruption, enables price comparison, backup if one fails — BUT more admin, smaller discounts per order, harder to build close relationships. Application expected: small scale, perishable goods, local reputation at stake. Mastering (7-9): balanced discussion, application to a bakery context, supported judgement. Secure (5-6): both sides considered with application, limited judgement. Developing (3-4): one side developed, other side mentioned. Emerging (1-2): single side or generic theory only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of organic growth?
A) A supermarket buying a rival supermarket chain
B) Two banks agreeing to merge
C) A coffee chain opening a new branch using retained profit
D) A car maker taking over a tyre manufacturer
practice_questions.marks:
C) A coffee chain opening a new branch using retained profit [1 mark]
Organic growth is funded internally without merging with or buying another business. Options A, B and D all describe external growth.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of external growth named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: merger, takeover. Accept also: horizontal, vertical, diversification (as types of merger/takeover direction). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way in which a supermarket could grow organically. (Context: a mid-sized UK supermarket chain based in the North West wants to grow without buying any other businesses.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a named route to organic growth (e.g. increasing output, gaining new customers, developing new products, or increasing market share).
2 marks: adds brief development AND applies to the supermarket scenario.
Indicative answer: ‘The supermarket could develop new own-label products (1) such as a plant-based range, attracting vegan shoppers in the North West without needing to buy a rival chain (1).’ [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business might choose external growth rather than organic growth.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. speed, instant market share, access to expertise, reducing competition).
2 marks: develops the reason logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked point, often a consequence for the business.
Indicative answer: ‘External growth is much faster than organic growth (1), because buying a rival brings the customers, stores and staff in a single deal rather than opening new shops one at a time (2). This lets the business reach a target size in months rather than years, which matters when a rival might otherwise beat them to the market (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket of taking over a farm that supplies its vegetables. (Context: a large UK supermarket has just agreed a £90 million deal to buy a chain of farms in Lincolnshire.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from the vertical takeover and end with named, applied consequences for the supermarket. Sustained use of the scenario (Lincolnshire farms, £90m, vegetable supply) throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear cause-effect linkage and some application.
Developing: One chain developed, limited application to the scenario.
Emerging: Simple points with little development or scenario use.
Indicative content:
- Control over supply → more reliable vegetable stock on shelves → fewer gaps → better customer experience, protecting market share in competitive grocery sector.
- Backward vertical integration → cuts the middle-man margin → lower unit cost of vegetables → the supermarket can hold prices down against rivals like Aldi or Lidl.
Counterweights candidates may credit: £90m deal is a sunk cost that cannot be undone if consumer demand falls; farming is a new industry with unfamiliar risks (weather, disease, land regulation). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a fast-growing UK craft brewery should grow organically or by taking over a smaller rival. (Context: a craft brewery founded in Leeds in 2018 has grown to 40 staff and is now choosing between (A) building a second brewery from scratch in Manchester or (B) buying a smaller independent brewery in Liverpool that has an established customer base but outdated kit.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments on both options applied directly to the craft brewery. Supported judgement that weighs one factor as most important (e.g. speed vs control) or uses an ‘it depends on X’ framing with X justified.
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear recommendation, some application.
Developing: Some points on both sides with limited development; conclusion restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported judgement.

Arguments for organic (A): full control over the new site, no overpayment risk, brand consistency protected, lower upfront cost, builds in-house team capability.
Arguments for takeover (B): instant customer base in Liverpool, quicker route into a new city, existing staff who know local pubs and tastes, faster growth to fight off bigger craft brands.
Against organic: slower, may miss market window, Manchester build could overrun on cost.
Against takeover: outdated kit in Liverpool needs replacing, culture clash between Leeds founders and Liverpool staff, risk of overpaying.
Judgement: credit students who note the decision depends on how fast rivals are expanding and whether the brewery’s cash can absorb the takeover price. Unsupported judgements (‘I think option A is better’) cap below the top band. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of marketing?
A) Producing goods as cheaply as possible
B) Keeping accurate financial records
C) Identifying customers and meeting their needs to increase sales
D) Training staff to use new machinery
practice_questions.marks:
C) Identifying customers and meeting their needs to increase sales [1 mark]
Marketing is about customers, not production, finance or training. Options A, B and D describe operations, finance and HR.

practice_questions.text: State one purpose of marketing named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: identifying customers, understanding customers, informing customers, increasing sales. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason why a business needs to understand its customers. (Context: a small UK bakery chain is planning to launch a new range of pastries.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. to design the right product, to avoid wasted spending, to stay ahead of rivals).
2 marks: adds brief development AND applies to the bakery.
Indicative answer: ‘Understanding customers helps the bakery choose flavours customers actually want (1), avoiding the cost of baking pastries that sit unsold (1).’ [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which marketing can help a business to increase sales. (Context: an independent coffee shop in Bristol has seen sales flatten over the past year.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a way marketing increases sales (e.g. informing customers through social media, launching a new product after research, offering promotions).
2 marks: develops the point logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked development applied to the Bristol coffee shop.
Indicative answer: ‘The shop could use social media to inform local customers about a new seasonal drink (1). This reaches a wider audience than relying on walk-by foot traffic alone (2), which should pull new students and young workers into the shop and lift sales again (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how identifying its customers helps a new UK business. (Context: a Leeds-based start-up is launching a range of plant-based ready meals aimed at health-conscious students.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from identifying the target customer (health-conscious Leeds students) and end in a named business outcome. Sustained use of the scenario throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear cause-effect, some application.
Developing: One chain developed; limited application.
Emerging: Lists benefits of identifying customers without applying to the scenario.
Indicative chains:
- Identifying the target customer → knows flavours and portion sizes that suit students → product designed to fit student lifestyles → higher sales and less wasted stock.
- Identifying the customer → chooses promotion channels students actually use (TikTok, university Instagram) → cheaper marketing spend → more revenue per pound spent.
Application hooks the scenario offers: Leeds, students, plant-based, health-conscious, ready meal format. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of the four purposes of marketing for a new small UK business. (Context: two friends are opening a new vegan cafe in a busy university city and only have £12,000 to spend on their launch.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed arguments on why each purpose matters, balanced against limits and trade-offs, applied throughout to the vegan cafe and the £12,000 budget. Supported judgement on which purposes matter most.
Secure: Developed arguments on most purposes with some application and a clear judgement.
Developing: Some purposes explained but limited application; judgement weak or missing.
Emerging: Lists purposes without developing or applying.

Arguments for importance: identifying customers saves the £12,000 budget from being wasted on the wrong group; understanding customers lets the cafe design a menu students actually want; informing customers through social media is cheap and effective for a start-up; the point of it all is to increase sales and survive the first year.
Limits: a small business can also succeed by word of mouth alone; spending too much on research eats into the £12,000; some purposes matter more than others early on.
Judgement: credit candidates who weight identifying and understanding as most important early on (because you cannot fix a wrong customer with a bigger budget), with informing and sales growing over time. Unsupported conclusions cap below the top band. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is NOT a typical job of the finance function?
A) Paying supplier invoices
B) Designing a new logo
C) Producing a cash flow forecast
D) Running the payroll
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for selecting option B (Designing a new logo). No marks for any other answer.

practice_questions.text: State one piece of financial information produced by the finance function.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid answer: income statement, cash flow forecast, statement of financial position, budget report, sales/revenue report, payroll summary, gross/net profit figure. Precise term required.

practice_questions.text: Outline one way the finance function supports business planning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid way (setting budgets / forecasting cash flow / producing financial statements / assessing the affordability of a plan). 1 mark for a brief development linking the activity to better planning. Mastering: precise way with clear development. Secure: valid way with some development. Developing: way stated without development. Emerging: vague or partial point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the finance function is important to a growing UK business such as Gymshark.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid reason (cash flow management / securing investment / tracking growing costs / supporting decisions as the business scales). 1 mark for applying to Gymshark’s context (rapid growth / high marketing spend / international expansion). 1 mark for a developed chain (e.g. ‘without accurate cash flow forecasts, Gymshark might overspend on new product lines and run out of cash to pay suppliers’). Mastering: developed chain tied to context. Secure: reason with application. Developing: reason with weak application. Emerging: reason stated only.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the finance function could help the marketing team at a business like Innocent Drinks make better decisions.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: finance provides a marketing budget → team plans campaigns within what business can afford; finance tracks return on spend → identifies which campaigns generate most sales per pound → future campaigns focus on highest-return channels; finance produces sales data broken down by product → marketing targets growing segments, drops declining ones; finance forecasts cash → marketing times launches when cash is available. Mastering (5-6): developed chains of reasoning tying finance activity to a concrete marketing decision, applied to Innocent. Secure (3-4): clear reasoning with some application. Developing (2): partial reasoning, limited application. Emerging (1): identifies a link without chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the extent to which a small start-up business truly needs a dedicated finance function.
practice_questions.marks: Candidates should weigh both sides. In favour: finance ensures tax is paid on time, cash flow is monitored, profit is tracked accurately, and growth is planned realistically — poor bookkeeping is a common reason start-ups fail. Against: a dedicated function is expensive; software like Xero and QuickBooks automates much of the work; the owner often knows the numbers intimately; money spent on a full-time accountant could fund marketing or stock instead. A balanced answer might distinguish between a sole trader using software versus a fast-growing start-up needing a part-time bookkeeper. Mastering (7-9): balanced discussion with application and supported judgement. Secure (5-6): both sides with application, limited judgement. Developing (3-4): one side developed, other mentioned. Emerging (1-2): single side or generic theory only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of secondary research?
A) Running a focus group with target customers
B) Reading Office for National Statistics data on household income
C) Interviewing a new supplier
D) Trialling a new ready meal in ten stores
practice_questions.marks:
B) Reading Office for National Statistics data on household income [1 mark]
The census is one of OCR’s named secondary sources. Options A, C and D are all primary research (new information collected by the business).

practice_questions.text: Identify one primary research method named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: questionnaires, interviews, trialling, focus groups. Do NOT accept secondary sources (newspapers, census, websites, internal data) — those are secondary. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A cafe has total sales of £150,000. The total value of the local cafe market is £1,500,000. Calculate the cafe’s market share. You must show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: correct method shown (150,000 ÷ 1,500,000) × 100 or equivalent.
2 marks: correct final answer of 10%, with units.
Accept: 10%, 10.0%, 0.1 × 100. Do not accept 10 without % sign unless working clearly shows percentage. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of trialling a new product before a national launch. (Context: a UK food manufacturer is considering a new plant-based ready meal.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies an advantage (e.g. real customer feedback, reduces risk of flop, chance to tweak recipe).
2 marks: develops the point logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked development applied to the food manufacturer.
Indicative answer: ‘Trialling the ready meal in a small number of stores gives the manufacturer real sales data rather than opinions (1). Customers are buying with their own money, so their reaction shows true demand, not polite answers in a survey (2). The recipe and packaging can then be tweaked before a national rollout, reducing the risk that the full launch loses money (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how internal data could help a UK supermarket chain make better marketing decisions. (Context: a regional supermarket chain is reviewing its loyalty card and EPOS till data from the past year.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from internal data (EPOS / loyalty card) and end with named, applied consequences for the supermarket. Sustained use of scenario throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear cause-effect and some application.
Developing: One chain developed, limited scenario use.
Emerging: Lists uses of internal data without applying to the supermarket.
Indicative chains:
- EPOS till data → shows which products sell at which times → supermarket restocks the best-selling items earlier each week → fewer gaps on shelves → higher customer satisfaction and repeat sales.
- Loyalty card data → reveals which segments buy plant-based products → targeted email promotions to those customers → higher response rate than generic advertising → lower cost per sale.
Credit candidates who note internal data is free compared with external research, or who raise its limits (only tells the business about current customers, not potential new ones). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a new small UK cafe should rely mostly on primary or secondary research before launching. (Context: two friends are opening an independent cafe in a busy university town with £8,000 of launch budget, most of which is committed to rent and equipment.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed arguments on both primary and secondary research, applied throughout to the cafe and the £8,000 budget, with a supported judgement.
Secure: Developed arguments on both, clear judgement, some application.
Developing: Some points on both but weakly developed; judgement limited.
Emerging: Lists features without weighing.

Arguments for secondary: cheap or free, quick, already exists (census data on the student population, Mintel reports on cafe trends, competitor websites), leaves most of the £8,000 for rent and equipment.
Arguments for primary: specific to the cafe (taste preferences in THIS town, price sensitivity of THESE students), gives honest reactions to the menu, no published report covers one independent cafe.
Drawbacks: secondary may be out of date or too general; primary costs time and money the cafe cannot afford at scale.
Judgement: strong candidates recommend a mix — free secondary first (census, Mintel, competitor websites) to set the market context, then low-cost primary (Instagram polls, counter chats, a trial weekend) to test the menu. Credit for supported judgement weighted by budget reality. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an internal source of finance?
A) Bank loan
B) Trade credit
C) Retained profit
D) Crowdfunding
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for selecting option C (Retained profit). No marks for any other answer.

practice_questions.text: State one source of finance only available to a limited company.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for ‘share issue’ (or ‘new share issue’). No other answer accepted. Crowdfunding alone is not accepted as sole traders can also crowdfund.

practice_questions.text: A small café needs £4,000 to buy a new coffee machine. Calculate how much the café will repay if it takes a bank loan of £4,000 over 2 years at a total interest charge of 12% of the original loan.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for interest calculation: £4,000 × 0.12 = £480. 1 mark for total repayment: £4,000 + £480 = £4,480 (with £ unit). Method marks credited: if interest wrongly calculated, correct addition still earns 1 mark. Correct final answer with unit = full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a new sole trader might choose to use owner’s capital rather than a bank loan to fund their start-up.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid reason (no trading history so bank may refuse / avoids interest payments / keeps full control / faster than loan approval). 1 mark for application to a sole trader context (no collateral / no track record / small sums). 1 mark for developed chain (e.g. ‘a new sole trader has no sales history, so a bank sees them as high risk and may reject a loan application — using savings avoids this refusal’). Mastering: developed chain tied to context. Secure: reason with application. Developing: reason with weak application. Emerging: reason stated only.

practice_questions.text: A business has forecast profit of £180,000 this year. It plans to pay £60,000 to its owners and keep the rest as retained profit. Calculate (a) the retained profit this year, and (b) the percentage of profit retained.
practice_questions.marks: (a) Retained profit: £180,000 − £60,000 = £120,000 (2 marks; 1 for correct method, 1 for answer with £ unit). (b) Percentage: £120,000 ÷ £180,000 × 100 = 66.67% (or 66.7% / 67%) (2 marks; 1 for correct method, 1 for answer with % unit). Full method marks available even if one figure is wrong. Answer stated with correct unit essential.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the most suitable source of finance for a growing UK company like BrewDog to fund a new overseas brewery costing £5 million.
practice_questions.marks: Candidates should weigh at least two realistic options and reach a supported judgement. Share issue/crowdfunding: can raise large sums, no fixed repayment, builds community (BrewDog historically used Equity for Punks) — BUT dilutes ownership, complex to set up. Bank loan: keeps ownership, interest tax-deductible, straightforward — BUT £5m is large, requires collateral, fixed repayments hurt cash flow if brewery underperforms. Retained profit: no interest, fast — BUT £5m may exceed reserves, leaves no buffer. Application to BrewDog expected. Mastering (7-9): balanced discussion, application to BrewDog, supported judgement naming the source and why. Secure (5-6): both sides with some application, limited judgement. Developing (3-4): one side developed, other mentioned. Emerging (1-2): single side or generic theory only.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is most likely to be a fixed cost for a bakery?
A) Flour used in each loaf
B) Packaging for each cake
C) Monthly rent on the shop
D) Electricity used to run ovens per batch
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for selecting option C (Monthly rent on the shop). No marks for any other answer.

practice_questions.text: State the formula for calculating net profit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: ‘Net profit = Gross profit − Other expenses’ (or equivalent wording: Net profit = Revenue − Cost of sales − Other expenses). Must show full deduction.

practice_questions.text: A bakery sells 500 loaves at £2.40 each. Calculate its total revenue.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for method: £2.40 × 500. 1 mark for answer: £1,200 (with £ unit). Bare number 1,200 without unit = 1 mark only. Correct answer with unit = full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business might want to distinguish between gross profit and net profit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid reason (each shows a different part of the business performance / net profit reveals the impact of overheads / investors compare both to judge efficiency). 1 mark for application to business context (e.g. a shop, a manufacturer). 1 mark for developed chain (e.g. ‘a business with high gross profit but low net profit has a pricing problem versus one with low gross profit that has a cost-of-sales problem’). Mastering: developed chain tied to context. Secure: reason with application. Developing: reason only. Emerging: vague point.

practice_questions.text: A business has revenue of £300,000, cost of sales of £180,000 and other expenses of £90,000. Calculate (a) gross profit, (b) net profit, (c) net profit as a percentage of revenue.
practice_questions.marks: (a) Gross profit: £300,000 − £180,000 = £120,000 (1 mark with £ unit). (b) Net profit: £120,000 − £90,000 = £30,000 (1 mark with £ unit, follow-through from (a) allowed). (c) Net profit %: £30,000 ÷ £300,000 × 100 = 10% (2 marks; 1 for correct method, 1 for answer with % unit). Full method credit even if (a) or (b) wrong. Units essential on each final answer.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a fall in sales would affect a cinema with high fixed costs compared to a market-stall sandwich seller with low fixed costs.
practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: cinema has high fixed costs (building, staff, projector) → these must be paid even if ticket sales fall → small drop in sales quickly wipes out profit and pushes it into loss; market stall has low fixed costs (stall rent only) → fall in sales cuts variable costs proportionally → business stays break-even or only mildly loss-making; cinema is therefore far more sensitive to demand swings → needs bigger cash reserves / aggressive promotion; sandwich seller can scale back more safely. Mastering (5-6): developed chain with comparison and second-order consequence. Secure (3-4): clear reasoning with comparison. Developing (2): partial reasoning, one-sided. Emerging (1): identifies an effect without chain of reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a segmentation base named in the specification?
A) Age
B) Income
C) Favourite sport
D) Lifestyle
practice_questions.marks:
C) Favourite sport [1 mark]
The five named bases are age, gender, income, location and lifestyle. Favourite sport is not a spec-listed base, although it could be considered part of a lifestyle segment in practice.

practice_questions.text: Identify one segmentation base a UK holiday company might use to target customers aged 50 and over.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: age. Do not accept other bases unless clearly justified as relevant to over-50s. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way in which a UK clothing business could use lifestyle segmentation. (Context: a new UK clothing brand wants to target customers who train at the gym regularly.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies how lifestyle segmentation is being used (e.g. targeting active gym-goers with fitted sportswear).
2 marks: adds brief development AND applies to the clothing brand.
Indicative answer: ‘The brand could design fitted training clothes for regular gym-goers (1), promoting them through fitness influencers on Instagram rather than traditional TV adverts, reaching the active lifestyle segment where they already spend their time (1).’ [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a UK supermarket might segment the market by income.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. to target price-conscious shoppers, to justify premium pricing, to choose store locations).
2 marks: develops the reason logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked development, applied to the supermarket.
Indicative answer: ‘Income segmentation lets the supermarket decide which product range to offer (1). Aldi targets lower-income households with a no-frills own-brand range and keeps prices low (2). This reduces the risk of trying to compete on quality with Waitrose and wins a loyal customer base by being clearly cheapest in the market (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how using lifestyle segmentation can benefit a new UK fitness brand. (Context: Gymshark, a Bromsgrove-founded fitness clothing brand, targets customers who train regularly and follow fitness influencers on social media.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from lifestyle segmentation and end with named, applied consequences for Gymshark (or the brand in the question). Sustained use of the scenario throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear cause-effect and some application.
Developing: One chain developed; limited scenario use.
Emerging: Lists benefits of lifestyle segmentation without applying.
Indicative chains:
- Lifestyle segmentation → designs fitted gym clothes that suit training → customers feel the product is ‘for them’ → strong brand loyalty → repeat sales.
- Targeting gym-goers who follow influencers → marketing through Instagram fitness creators → cheaper than TV ads and reaches the exact audience → higher return on marketing spend.
Credit candidates who note that lifestyle segmentation allowed Gymshark to grow from a garage to over £1 billion valuation by owning one tight segment. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether segmenting customers by lifestyle is more useful than segmenting by age for a new UK streaming service. (Context: a UK start-up is planning a paid video streaming service and must choose how to target its first customers with a £1.5 million marketing budget.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments on both lifestyle and age segmentation, applied throughout to the streaming service and the £1.5m budget. Supported judgement that weights one base as more important or uses ‘it depends on X’ framing with X justified.
Secure: Developed arguments on both bases, clear recommendation, some application.
Developing: Some points on both but limited development; conclusion restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported judgement.

Arguments for lifestyle segmentation: captures viewing habits (binge-watchers, sport fans, documentary viewers) which directly shape what shows to buy; more relevant to streaming because two 30-year-olds with different lifestyles want very different content; lets the service position content on social platforms those lifestyles use.
Arguments for age segmentation: easier to measure and target (age is publicly captured in the census and by ad platforms); content ratings are built around age; older and younger viewers differ sharply on price sensitivity and device use.
Drawbacks: lifestyle data is harder and slower to gather than age data, costing more of the £1.5m. Age alone misses the fact that a 70-year-old and a 25-year-old can share the same streaming habits.
Judgement: credit candidates who argue that a combination is strongest — a streaming service should use age for broad channel choice (TikTok for younger, Facebook for older) and lifestyle for content targeting. Pure one-base answers cap below the top band. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the SECOND stage of the product life cycle?
A) Decline
B) Growth
C) Maturity
D) Introduction
practice_questions.marks:
B) Growth [1 mark]
The order of the four stages is introduction, growth, maturity, decline. Growth comes second.

practice_questions.text: State the four stages of the product life cycle in order.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all four in the correct order: introduction, growth, maturity, decline. Any missing or out of order scores 0. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between invention and innovation. (Context: Dyson designed the first bagless vacuum cleaner in 1993, then has released improved models every few years since.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies the distinction (invention = genuinely new; innovation = improvement on something existing).
2 marks: adds development AND applies to the Dyson scenario.
Indicative answer: ‘The original 1993 bagless vacuum was an invention because no such product existed (1). Later Dyson models are innovations — they improve features such as suction or battery life but do not create a new category (1).’ [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one action a business might take when a product reaches the maturity stage.
practice_questions.marks:
