1 mark: identifies an action (e.g. refresh the product, cut the price, add new features, new packaging, new target market).
2 marks: develops the action logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked development, often a consequence for the business.
Indicative answer: ‘At maturity, sales flatten and the business might refresh the product (1). Cadbury Dairy Milk has added Fruit & Nut, Caramel and plant-based versions to give customers a new reason to buy (2). This keeps the brand in maturity for longer and delays the decline stage, protecting revenue (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how understanding the product life cycle could benefit a UK smartphone business. (Context: a UK smartphone company has an older model that sold well for three years but whose sales have flattened in the past twelve months.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from the product life cycle and end with named, applied consequences for the smartphone business. Sustained scenario use.
Secure: Two developed chains with cause-effect and some application.
Developing: One chain developed; limited application.
Emerging: Lists stages without applying to the scenario.
Indicative chains:
- Recognising that flat sales mean maturity → triggers a product refresh (new features, a cheaper version, bundled accessories) → sales extended for another year → revenue protected while the next model is developed.
- Recognising maturity → business avoids increasing advertising spend wastefully → budget redirected to the next model’s introduction → healthier portfolio, with one product earning and one growing.
Credit candidates who note the risk of misreading the stage — treating a growth product as mature leads to under-investment and missed sales. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a UK drinks company should invest in a brand-new invention or focus on innovating its existing range. (Context: a UK drinks company already sells a successful range of flavoured waters and is choosing between (A) launching a completely new, protein-enhanced sports drink, or (B) adding three new flavours and updated packaging to the existing flavoured water range.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments on invention (A) and innovation (B), applied directly to the drinks company. Supported judgement that weights one option or uses an ‘it depends on X’ framing with X justified.
Secure: Developed arguments on both options, clear recommendation, some application.
Developing: Some points on both with limited development; conclusion restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported judgement.

Arguments for invention (A): higher reward if successful, enters the growing sports drink market, stronger brand story, potential to patent a new formulation, attracts new customers outside the current range.
Arguments for innovation (B): far lower risk (existing flavoured water range is already mature), faster to market, uses existing supply chain and retail relationships, refreshes the range and extends its maturity stage, cheaper to promote because the brand is already known.
Drawbacks: invention needs heavy R&D spend and may flop against established rivals (Lucozade, Powerade); innovation may fail to excite customers if the flavours are not genuinely different.
Judgement: strong candidates argue that innovation (B) is the safer short-term play, while invention (A) may be worth pursuing on the side if the company has the cash reserves. Credit for ‘it depends on cash reserves and competitor activity’ framing with clear support. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct formula for net profit margin?
A) (Net profit ÷ Gross profit) × 100
B) (Net profit ÷ Revenue) × 100
C) (Revenue ÷ Net profit) × 100
D) (Net profit ÷ Total costs) × 100
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for selecting option B ((Net profit ÷ Revenue) × 100). No marks for any other answer.

practice_questions.text: State what ARR stands for and what unit it is expressed in.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark only if both elements correct: ‘Average Rate of Return, expressed as a percentage (%)’. Missing either element = 0 marks.

practice_questions.text: A business has revenue of £500,000 and gross profit of £200,000. Calculate its gross profit margin.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for method: (£200,000 ÷ £500,000) × 100. 1 mark for answer: 40% (with % unit). Bare number 40 without % = 1 mark only. Full method credit if arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business might prefer to look at net profit margin rather than gross profit margin.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for valid reason (net profit margin reflects all costs / shows true profitability after overheads / investors and lenders use it to judge performance). 1 mark for applying to a business context. 1 mark for developed chain (e.g. ‘a business with healthy gross margin but weak net margin has an overhead problem, which gross margin alone would hide — so net margin is more useful for spotting cost pressure’). Mastering: developed chain tied to context. Secure: reason with application. Developing: reason only. Emerging: vague point.

practice_questions.text: A company invests £40,000 in a new machine. Over 4 years the machine generates total profit of £24,000. Calculate (a) the average annual profit, and (b) the Average Rate of Return.
practice_questions.marks: (a) Average annual profit: £24,000 ÷ 4 = £6,000 (2 marks; 1 for correct method, 1 for answer with £ unit). (b) ARR: (£6,000 ÷ £40,000) × 100 = 15% (2 marks; 1 for correct method, 1 for answer with % unit). Follow-through from (a) allowed. Units essential. Full method credit where working is clear even if arithmetic errs.

practice_questions.text: A business is considering two investment projects. Project A has an ARR of 25% but generates most of its profit in year 5. Project B has an ARR of 18% but generates profit evenly across its 5 years. Evaluate which project the business should choose.
practice_questions.marks: Candidates must weigh both projects and reach a supported judgement. Project A: higher % return, greater reward — BUT returns delayed, money locked up, cash flow strain in years 1-4, greater forecasting risk (year 5 may not happen), opportunity cost. Project B: lower % return — BUT steady cash flow helps pay bills, lower forecasting risk, more flexible if the business needs to pivot. Judgement criteria: cash position of business (strong cash = A preferable; tight cash = B), risk tolerance, alternative uses of money. Must acknowledge what ARR ignores (timing, risk). Mastering (8-9): balanced evaluation with application, supported judgement naming which project and key conditions. Secure (6-7): both projects weighed, partial judgement. Developing (4-5): one project developed, other mentioned. Emerging (1-3): single side or generic theory only.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct formula for the break-even point in units?
A) Fixed costs × Contribution per unit
B) Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit
C) Contribution per unit ÷ Fixed costs
D) Total revenue − Total costs
practice_questions.marks:
B) Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit [1 mark]
Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Options A and C reverse or multiply the formula; D is the definition of profit, not break-even.

practice_questions.text: State the formula for contribution per unit.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit.
Accept equivalent wording (e.g. ‘price minus variable cost per unit’). Do not accept contribution = revenue − total cost (that is profit). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A small bakery sells loaves at £3.00 each. The variable cost per loaf is £1.20. Fixed costs are £900 a week. Calculate the break-even quantity for the bakery.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: contribution per unit = £3.00 − £1.20 = £1.80.
2 marks: break-even = £900 ÷ £1.80 = 500 loaves per week.
Method marks are credited if contribution is correct even if the final division is wrong. Accept 500 loaves, 500 units, 500/week. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why break-even is useful for a small business owner when planning for the year ahead.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a use (e.g. setting a sales target, informing pricing, guiding marketing spend).
2 marks: adds linked development — e.g. ‘the owner knows the minimum weekly sales needed to cover all costs’.
3 marks: applies to a small business consequence — e.g. ‘so she can plan staffing levels and promotions around that target, reducing the risk of losses in quieter weeks’.
Indicative answer: ‘Break-even gives the owner a minimum sales target (1) below which the business makes a loss and above which it makes profit (2), so she can plan staff hours and marketing to reliably beat that number (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A café has fixed costs of £2,000 a month. It sells sandwiches at £5.00 each with a variable cost of £2.50 per sandwich. Calculate the break-even quantity, then calculate the new break-even quantity if the variable cost rises to £3.00. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: original contribution = £5.00 − £2.50 = £2.50.
2 marks: original break-even = £2,000 ÷ £2.50 = 800 sandwiches per month.
3 marks: new contribution = £5.00 − £3.00 = £2.00.
4 marks: new break-even = £2,000 ÷ £2.00 = 1,000 sandwiches per month.
Method marks credited for correct working even if arithmetic errors later. Units (sandwiches / per month) not required for marks but good practice. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a manufacturer’s break-even point if its fixed costs rise by 20%. (Context: a Midlands engineering firm has just renewed its factory lease on terms that push fixed costs from £50,000 to £60,000 a month. Contribution per unit is currently £25.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Chain of reasoning links the rise in fixed costs to a numerical shift in break-even (£50,000/£25 = 2,000 units to £60,000/£25 = 2,400 units, a 400-unit rise) and then to a consequence for the firm (e.g. larger sales target, pressure on margins, greater risk in slow months). Context sustained throughout.
Secure: Calculates the shift correctly and explains one developed consequence for the firm.
Developing: Recognises break-even rises but no calculation or weak application to the firm.
Emerging: Defines break-even or fixed costs without linking to the 20% rise or the firm.
Indicative content: higher fixed costs → numerator of formula rises → break-even rises to 2,400 units → firm must sell 400 more units just to cover costs → less room for error if orders fall short. A generic answer with no figures or no reference to the Midlands firm cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes penetration pricing?
A. Setting a very high launch price and lowering it later.
B. Setting a low launch price to win market share, then raising it.
C. Adding a fixed percentage mark-up to unit cost.
D. Matching competitors’ prices exactly.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct letter (B) clearly indicated. Secure: Correct letter selected. Developing: Incorrect letter. Emerging: No response or multiple unclear responses. (1 mark for B.)

practice_questions.text: State one pricing method a business could use when launching a new, innovative smartphone with features no rival offers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a valid method precisely (price skimming). Secure: Names price skimming or an accepted equivalent term. Developing: Names a pricing concept that is not skimming but is related (e.g. premium). Emerging: No valid term given. (1 mark for price skimming.)

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason a new subscription streaming service entering the UK might use penetration pricing.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear point (win market share quickly) plus a developed feature or consequence (because the market already has established rivals like Netflix). Secure: Point plus brief feature. Developing: Single-word or one-line answer with no development. Emerging: Incorrect or missing. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason a small independent plumber might choose cost-plus pricing rather than competitor pricing.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cost-plus guarantees a margin (1), applies it to the small plumber scenario (1), and develops the reasoning with a ‘because’ clause tied to the business (e.g. small businesses need certainty on every job to stay solvent) (1). Secure: Two of the three elements. Developing: Knowledge only, no application. Emerging: No relevant response. (3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket of using loss leader promotional pricing on milk and bread.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Sustained chain of reasoning — loss leader draws footfall → customers fill the trolley with higher-margin items → overall basket profit rises even though milk loses money → plus recognition of risk (e.g. customers cherry-picking the loss leaders and leaving). Secure (3-4): Clear chain with application to a supermarket but limited development or one-sided. Developing (1-2): Descriptive, lists points, little chain of reasoning. Emerging (0): No relevant analysis. (6 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A new UK craft gin brand is deciding between price skimming and penetration pricing for its launch in supermarkets. Recommend which method it should use. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Clear recommendation supported by two developed reasons, both applied to the craft gin context (e.g. crowded spirits market with established rivals favours penetration for visibility), weighs at least one counter-point (skimming risk that rivals copy quickly), and ends with a supported judgement tied to the scenario. Secure (6-7): Recommendation with application and some evaluation but thinner judgement. Developing (3-5): Recommendation with limited application, largely descriptive. Emerging (1-2): Generic answer with no clear recommendation. (0) No response. (9 marks.)

practice_questions.text:
Which of these is a form of digital distribution?
A. A Primark high-street store.
B. The ASOS website.
C. A branch of Greggs.
D. A market stall in Manchester.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct letter (B) clearly indicated. Secure: Correct letter selected. Developing: Incorrect letter. Emerging: No response. (1 mark for B.)

practice_questions.text: Identify one advertising channel named on the specification.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names one valid channel precisely (TV, radio, print, websites, or social media). Secure: Names a valid channel. Developing: Names a promotional method but not an advertising channel (e.g. ‘free sample’). Emerging: No valid response. (1 mark.)

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason a new independent coffee shop might choose social media rather than television advertising.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear point (social media is much cheaper, or reaches local customers precisely) plus development. Secure: Point plus brief feature. Developing: One-line or unsupported answer. Emerging: No valid response. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a UK fashion retailer of using digital distribution alongside its high-street stores.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a benefit (e.g. reaches customers 24/7 or opens international markets) (1), applies it to a fashion retailer (1), and develops with a ‘because’ clause tied to the scenario (1). Secure: Two elements present. Developing: Knowledge only, no application. Emerging: No relevant response. (3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket of running a free sample promotion for a new ready-meal range in its stores.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Sustained chain — free samples let customers try without risk → some convert to buyers → builds awareness of the new range faster than adverts alone → plus recognition of cost (samples cost money, some customers will try and not buy). Secure (3-4): Clear chain with some application. Developing (1-2): Descriptive list of points. Emerging (0): No relevant analysis. (6 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a new UK online-only clothing brand should spend most of its promotional budget on Instagram influencers or on television advertising.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-9): Both sides developed — Instagram reaches target customer cheaply and allows targeting; TV reaches mass audience and builds brand faster but costs much more. Applied to an online-only clothing brand. Ends with supported judgement. Secure (5-6): Both sides with application but thinner evaluation. Developing (3-4): One side only, limited application. Emerging (1-2): Generic points. (0) No response. (9 marks.)

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct formula for net cash flow?
A) Opening balance + closing balance
B) Revenue − total costs
C) Cash inflows − cash outflows
D) Profit − tax
practice_questions.marks:
C) Cash inflows − cash outflows [1 mark]
Net cash flow is the simple difference between cash in and cash out for the period. A describes balances, B describes profit, D describes post-tax profit.

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why a profitable business can still run out of cash.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of:
- customers pay on credit so cash arrives later than the sale
- heavy spending on stock or equipment ties up cash
- seasonal dips mean outflows continue while inflows fall
- the business is growing too fast to fund from current cash.
Accept any valid cause tied to timing of cash vs. profit. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A business has an opening balance of £4,000 in March. Cash inflows are £9,000 and cash outflows are £11,500. Calculate the closing balance for March.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: net cash flow = £9,000 − £11,500 = −£2,500.
2 marks: closing balance = £4,000 + (−£2,500) = £1,500.
Accept £1,500 or 1,500. Method marks credited if net cash flow correct even if the final addition is wrong. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a cash-flow forecast is useful to the owner of a small business.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a use (e.g. anticipating shortages, providing targets, supporting a loan application).
2 marks: adds linked development — e.g. ‘the owner can see which months will be tight before they arrive’.
3 marks: applies to a consequence for the small business — e.g. ‘so she can arrange an overdraft in advance instead of panicking when the shortfall hits, keeping suppliers paid on time’.
Indicative answer: ‘A forecast shows predicted shortfalls early (1), so the owner can negotiate with suppliers or arrange an overdraft in advance (2), which means the business can keep paying wages and bills on time when the tight month arrives (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A cake shop has the following forecast for June: opening balance £2,500; inflows £8,000; outflows £9,800. For July, forecast inflows are £7,500 and outflows £8,200. Calculate the closing balance for June AND the closing balance for July. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: June net cash flow = £8,000 − £9,800 = −£1,800.
2 marks: June closing balance = £2,500 + (−£1,800) = £700.
3 marks: July net cash flow = £7,500 − £8,200 = −£700.
4 marks: July closing balance = £700 + (−£700) = £0.
Full method marks credited for correct working even if arithmetic slips. Accept any currency notation. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the likely impact on a small café of two months of negative net cash flow. (Context: a Newcastle café has just seen two consecutive months where cash outflows exceeded inflows by around £2,000 a month, largely due to a supplier price rise and a quieter summer than expected.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced answer weighing multiple impacts (pressure on liquidity, risk of missing wages/rent, possible need for an overdraft, damage to supplier relationships if payments delayed) with two-sided reasoning and a supported judgement tied to the café’s specific situation — e.g. ‘the shortfall is small and the cause is seasonal, so an overdraft plus one supplier renegotiation is likely enough; but if the quiet season extends, cost cutting becomes essential’.
Secure: Two impacts with development, at least one counterpoint, clear application to the Newcastle café.
Developing: One or two impacts, limited development, some application.
Emerging: Lists effects of negative cash flow without applying them to the café.
Indicative content: liquidity threatened → risk of late wages/rent → possible overdraft to bridge → interest cost → margin squeeze; supplier renegotiation → longer credit → keeps cash but risks supplier goodwill. Generic responses without reference to the café cannot score above 4. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes an integrated marketing mix?
A. A business that sells both in shops and online.
B. A mix where all four Ps send the same message to the target customer.
C. A mix that focuses mainly on promotion.
D. A business that uses several suppliers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct letter (B) clearly indicated. Secure: Correct letter selected. Developing: Incorrect letter. Emerging: No response. (1 mark for B.)

practice_questions.text: A business had 15% market share in 2023 and 12% market share in 2025. Calculate the percentage-point fall in its market share.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct answer (3 percentage points) with working shown (15 − 12 = 3). Secure: Correct answer, limited working. Developing: Wrong final answer but evidence of some correct method (e.g. subtraction set up). Emerging: Blank or clearly wrong. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason why falling weekly sales might prompt a business to change its marketing mix.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear point (falling sales signal the mix no longer matches what customers want) plus a brief development. Secure: Point with limited development. Developing: One-line answer. Emerging: No valid response. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a rise in a rival’s market share could affect the marketing mix of a UK supermarket.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a mix response (e.g. matching rival prices, refreshing own-brand range) (1), applies to a UK supermarket scenario (1), and develops with a ‘because’ clause (1). Secure: Two elements. Developing: Knowledge only. Emerging: No relevant response. (3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A coffee chain spent £40,000 on an Instagram campaign. Weekly sales rose from £180,000 to £216,000 during the campaign. Calculate the percentage change in weekly sales during the campaign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): Correct method shown — change £36,000 (1), divided by original £180,000 (1), × 100 (1), final answer 20% with unit (1). Secure (3): Correct final answer with some working. Developing (2): Correct method but wrong final figure. Emerging (0-1): No valid method or blank. (4 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A UK high-street fashion retailer is losing market share to online-only rivals. Recommend one change to its marketing mix. Justify your recommendation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Clear recommendation (e.g. invest in digital distribution, refresh promotion for social media) with two developed reasons applied to the retailer, weighs one counter-point (e.g. high-street brand identity, cost of new platform), ends with a supported judgement tied to the data in the scenario. Secure (6-7): Recommendation with application and some evaluation. Developing (3-5): Recommendation with limited application. Emerging (1-2): Generic answer, no clear recommendation. (9 marks.)

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the best example of sustainability in business?
A) A supermarket doubling the number of single-use plastic bags it sells
B) A fishery protecting stocks so future generations can still fish
C) A courier using more diesel vans to speed up delivery
D) A factory dumping waste into a local river to cut costs
practice_questions.marks:
B) A fishery protecting stocks so future generations can still fish [1 mark]
Sustainability means using resources in a way that does not exhaust them. A, C and D all increase environmental damage.

practice_questions.text: Identify one ethical consideration a UK clothing retailer should make when choosing a supplier.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of:
- fair pay / avoiding below-minimum wages
- safe factory conditions
- no child labour / modern slavery
- timely payment
- environmental impact of materials.
Accept any sensible ethical criterion linked to supplier choice. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way in which a UK business could reduce its environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies an action (e.g. switch to electric delivery vehicles, use recyclable packaging, install energy-efficient lighting, source sustainable raw materials).
2 marks: develops the action with an impact — e.g. ‘switch to electric vans (1), which cuts carbon emissions and avoids London ULEZ charges (1)’.
Both steps needed for 2 marks. Accept any valid development linking action to environmental outcome. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a business of sourcing materials from Fairtrade suppliers.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a benefit (e.g. improved brand reputation, customer loyalty, ability to charge a premium price, early compliance with regulation).
2 marks: adds linked development — e.g. ‘customers who care about fair wages for farmers are willing to pay more for products with a Fairtrade label’.
3 marks: applies to a business outcome — e.g. ‘which lets the business charge a higher price and raise its profit margin despite the extra cost of the Fairtrade ingredients’.
Indicative answer: ‘Fairtrade sourcing improves brand reputation (1) because ethically-aware customers will pay more for products that support fair wages for farmers (2), which lets the business earn higher margins despite the higher supplier cost (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how unethical treatment of suppliers could affect a UK supermarket’s long-term success. (Context: a large UK supermarket has been criticised in the media for paying small farmers 90 days after delivery and cutting prices by 20% with one week’s notice.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning, each tracing the unethical behaviour through consequences to a long-term business impact (e.g. supplier goodwill lost → farmers refuse to supply → empty shelves → lost sales; media coverage → damaged brand → shoppers switch to rivals like the Co-op or Waitrose). Sustained context throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear linkage to long-term consequences for the supermarket.
Developing: Chain started but not fully linked; some context used.
Emerging: Lists unethical practices without analysing consequences or applying to the supermarket.
Indicative content: late payment → supplier cash-flow crisis → farmers refuse future orders → supply gaps → lost sales; bad press → reputational damage → shoppers switch → falling revenue. Generic answers without reference to the supermarket cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a small UK coffee shop should switch entirely to Fairtrade-certified beans. (Context: an independent Sheffield coffee shop currently buys standard beans at £7 per kg and is considering switching to Fairtrade at £10 per kg. The owner estimates a 10% rise in customers if she advertises the change.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated balanced argument weighing multiple factors (rising costs, higher-margin sell, reputational gain, local competition, customer income level) with two-sided reasoning and a supported judgement that weighs one factor over others for this specific shop — e.g. ‘for a Sheffield independent with a student and professional clientele, the reputational gain plus 10% customer lift likely outweighs the £3/kg cost rise; the switch is worthwhile PROVIDED she raises prices by 20p–30p a cup to protect margin’. Sustained application throughout.
Secure: Clear balanced argument with two or more developed chains, supported judgement applied to the shop, context sustained.
Developing: Some balance, limited development, partial application, weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or generic; lists points without weighing or applying.
Indicative content: cost rises from £7 to £10 per kg → 43% rise in bean cost → margin squeezed unless price raised; BUT 10% customer lift → higher revenue → positive brand association → loyalty. Judgement should weight on: customer willingness to pay, competition from chains, scale of the shop. Generic answers without reference to the Sheffield shop cannot score above 6. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a flat organisational structure?
A. Many layers of management and narrow spans of control.
B. Few layers of management and wide spans of control.
C. A structure where employees report to two managers at once.
D. A business with no managers at all.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct letter (B) clearly indicated. Secure: Correct letter selected. Developing: Incorrect letter. Emerging: No response. (1 mark for B.)

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the ‘span of control’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise definition — the number of employees a manager is directly responsible for. Secure: Accurate but slightly reworded. Developing: Partial (‘how many people a manager has’ without ‘direct report’). Emerging: No valid response. (1 mark.)

practice_questions.text: Outline one benefit to a UK supermarket of employing part-time staff.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear point (match staffing to peak times) plus development tied to a supermarket (busy lunchtimes, evenings, weekends). Secure: Point with limited development. Developing: One-line answer. Emerging: No valid response. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a large NHS hospital trust might use a tall organisational structure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a reason (clear chain of responsibility for safety-critical decisions) (1), applies to the NHS hospital scenario (1), develops with a ‘because’ clause (errors in clinical decisions can cost lives) (1). Secure: Two elements. Developing: Knowledge only. Emerging: No relevant response. (3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK software firm of allowing employees to work from home full-time.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Sustained chain — remote working cuts office rent costs → widens the talent pool beyond commuting distance → can improve retention because staff save on travel → balanced by risk to collaboration, training and new-joiner integration. Secure (3-4): Clear chain with some application. Developing (1-2): Descriptive list. Emerging (0): No relevant analysis. (6 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether a fast-growing UK online retailer should use a flat organisational structure or move to a taller structure as it grows from 50 to 500 employees.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-9): Both sides developed — flat keeps speed and low management cost; tall adds control and clear supervision at larger scale. Applied to the growing online retailer. Ends with a supported judgement (e.g. move to tall in customer service and finance while keeping engineering flat). Secure (5-6): Both sides with application but thinner evaluation. Developing (3-4): One side only. Emerging (1-2): Generic. (0) No response. (9 marks.)

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes globalisation?
A) The closing of international trade borders
B) A business selling only in its home country
C) National economies becoming more connected through trade and investment
D) The government raising taxes on imports
practice_questions.marks:
C) National economies becoming more connected through trade and investment [1 mark]
Globalisation is the process of increased international connection. A is the opposite; B describes a purely domestic business; D is a trade policy, not globalisation.

practice_questions.text: State one effect of high unemployment on a UK high-street retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one of:
- falling sales / reduced consumer spending
- customers trading down to cheaper products
- easier / cheaper recruitment
- more competition from rivals closing down.
Accept any sensible effect tied specifically to unemployment. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way in which rising disposable income could affect a UK restaurant chain.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies the effect (e.g. rising sales, more bookings, higher spend per visit, ability to charge premium prices).
2 marks: develops with a linked consequence — e.g. ‘customers can afford to eat out more often (1), which lifts the chain’s revenue and allows it to open more branches (1)’.
Both the effect and the developed consequence needed for 2 marks. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the growth of multinationals has affected small UK businesses.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies an effect (e.g. increased competition on price, loss of local customers, opportunity to supply the multinational, cheaper access to technology).
2 marks: adds linked development — e.g. ‘Amazon can undercut independent bookshops because it buys in bulk and has lower overheads’.
3 marks: applies to a small-business consequence — e.g. ‘so many independents have closed as customers shift online, forcing survivors to focus on niche ranges or in-store experience to compete’.
Indicative answer: ‘Multinationals like Amazon compete on price (1) because their scale lets them undercut smaller rivals’ costs (2), so many independent UK bookshops have closed unless they specialise in rare titles or a community focus that Amazon cannot replicate (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact of a supply-chain crisis on a UK car manufacturer. (Context: a Midlands car plant has been told its computer-chip supplier in Taiwan is unable to deliver for six months due to a factory shutdown. The plant uses these chips in every vehicle built.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning, each tracing the supply disruption to a business consequence (e.g. no chips → production halts → lost sales → customers cancel orders or switch to rivals → long-term market share loss; idle factory → workers temporarily laid off or retained at full cost → margin crushed). Sustained context throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear consequences for the Midlands plant.
Developing: Chain started but not fully linked; some context.
Emerging: Describes the shortage without analysing consequences for the plant.
Indicative content: production stops → no cars to sell → revenue falls → margins hit; alternative supplier → higher costs → price rise or margin squeeze → customer backlash; delayed orders → brand damage → future sales at risk. Generic answers without reference to the Midlands plant cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a UK business selling non-essential goods could respond to a period of falling consumer income. (Context: a mid-sized UK clothing retailer with 40 stores has seen sales drop 12% as the 2023 cost-of-living squeeze bit into household budgets.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of multiple responses (price cuts, cheaper ranges, loyalty promotions, marketing changes, closing underperforming stores, extending credit) with two-sided reasoning and a supported judgement tied to the retailer. Sustained application.
Secure: Two or more developed responses, balance in reasoning, judgement linked to the retailer’s situation.
Developing: One or two responses, limited balance or development.
Emerging: Lists responses without weighing or applying.
Indicative content: introduce value range → retains trading-down customers but risks brand dilution; loyalty promotions → keeps existing customers but costs margin; close weakest stores → cuts fixed costs but risks redundancy and regional absence; extend finance options → lifts sales but raises bad-debt risk. Judgement: best mix depends on the retailer’s brand positioning and financial strength. Generic responses without reference to the retailer cannot score above 4. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the interdependent nature of business?
A) Each business function works completely independently
B) A decision in one function affects the other functions
C) A business only needs one function to succeed
D) All decisions must be made by the finance function
practice_questions.marks:
B) A decision in one function affects the other functions [1 mark]
Interdependence means the four functions (operations, finance, marketing, HR) all rely on each other. A is the opposite; C is wrong; D names a single function.

practice_questions.text: Identify the four main functions of a business.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for all four: operations, finance, marketing, human resources (HR).
Accept full names or ‘HR’ / ‘People’. All four must be named for the mark. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way in which the marketing function depends on the operations function.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies the dependency (e.g. marketing needs operations to deliver the product, meet supply, or hit quality targets).
2 marks: develops with a linked example — e.g. ‘marketing cannot promise a new product launch date (1) unless operations can scale production to meet expected demand on that day (1)’.
Both steps needed for 2. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which financial information supports decision making across a business.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a use (e.g. measuring whether a marketing campaign worked, checking production costs, monitoring cash, judging a price change).
2 marks: adds linked development — e.g. ‘sales and margin figures show whether the price supported by marketing is producing enough profit’.
3 marks: applies to a business outcome — e.g. ‘so managers can decide whether to extend the campaign, cut costs in operations, or change the price before the next quarter’.
Indicative answer: ‘Financial information like sales and margin figures (1) shows managers whether a marketing promotion is covering its cost and adding profit (2), which lets them decide whether to extend the campaign or pull it before more money is wasted (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a decision to launch a new product affects three different functions within a UK business. (Context: a mid-sized UK cereal brand has approved a new plant-based granola range for launch in six months. The board wants to know how the launch will affect operations, finance and HR.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked chains, one per function, each tracing the launch to a concrete business impact. Operations: new ingredient supply, factory line changes, quality testing → cost and capacity pressure. Finance: upfront cost, cash flow during ramp, margin target, break-even for the new range. HR: training, possible new hires, rotas around launch. Links between functions explicit. Sustained context.
Secure: Two or three functions with developed chains and clear linkage.
Developing: Functions named but chains short or weak.
Emerging: Lists tasks without chains or application.
Indicative content: operations → new production line → extra cost + risk of quality issues; finance → funding ramp → cash flow squeeze before sales arrive; HR → train staff + possibly hire → wage bill up. Generic answers without reference to the UK cereal brand cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a small UK café chain should open two new branches this year. (Context: a café chain with five branches in Bristol has £150,000 in retained profit. The owner is considering opening two more branches. Forecast ARR for each new branch is 22%; forecast break-even for each is 800 customer visits a week; each branch would need three new staff and a marketing launch.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated synoptic answer linking at least three functions (operations: site set-up, supply; finance: use of retained profit, ARR, break-even; marketing: local awareness; HR: hire and train six staff) with two-sided reasoning, explicit use of the numbers (22% ARR, 800 weekly break-even, £150,000 available), a supported judgement weighed for this specific chain — e.g. ‘open one branch first, prove the model, then open the second; 22% ARR beats any alternative investment, but spreading £150,000 across two simultaneous launches leaves no cushion if break-even slips’.
Secure: Clear balanced argument, three functions named, numbers used, judgement applied to the chain.
Developing: Partial linking, some function depth, weak use of numbers, basic judgement.
Emerging: One-sided or generic; lists points without weighing.
Indicative content: reward — 22% ARR beats savings rates, growth builds brand; risk — 800 visits/week break-even is steep for a new branch, £150,000 split across two leaves no emergency cash, HR load of hiring six trained staff simultaneously. Judgement options: open one then the second, open both, delay both, franchise instead. Generic answers without reference to the Bristol chain or the numbers cannot score above 6. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a non-financial method of motivation?
A. Performance-related bonus.
B. Profit-sharing scheme.
C. Staff discount at the company shop.
D. Job rotation to reduce boredom.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct letter (D) clearly indicated. Secure: Correct letter selected. Developing: Incorrect letter. Emerging: No response. (1 mark for D.)

practice_questions.text: Identify one method of selection a business could use alongside an interview.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names one valid method precisely (test, group activity, presentation, references, CV screen). Secure: Names a valid method. Developing: Names something unrelated (e.g. job advert). Emerging: No valid response. (1 mark.)

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between training and staff development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear point — training is short-term/narrow for the current role (1); development is longer-term/wider for future progression such as qualifications or apprenticeships (1). Secure: Distinction made but one side thinner. Developing: One side only or muddled. Emerging: No valid distinction. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a UK retailer of promoting internally rather than externally when filling a store manager role.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a benefit (e.g. faster, cheaper, motivates remaining staff) (1), applies to a UK retailer (1), develops with a ‘because’ clause (the promoted staff member already knows the store’s customers and processes) (1). Secure: Two elements. Developing: Knowledge only. Emerging: No relevant response. (3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK café chain of offering both financial (bonus) and non-financial (praise, job rotation) motivation methods.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Sustained chain — bonus rewards short-term sales targets → increases effort; non-financial methods reduce boredom and build belonging → raises retention → reduces recruitment cost overall. Applied to a café chain. Recognises trade-off (cost of bonus vs cheaper non-financial methods). Secure (3-4): Chain with some application. Developing (1-2): Descriptive list. Emerging (0): No relevant analysis. (6 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A fast-growing UK software firm must decide whether to invest most of its HR budget in short-term training courses or in longer-term staff development programmes such as apprenticeships and funded qualifications. Recommend which approach it should prioritise. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Clear recommendation with two developed reasons applied to a fast-growing software firm (e.g. apprenticeships build a pipeline of engineers as the firm scales), weighs at least one counter-point (short-term training is cheaper and fills immediate skill gaps), supported judgement tied to scenario, and correctly distinguishes training from development throughout. Secure (6-7): Recommendation with application and some evaluation. Developing (3-5): Recommendation with limited application, or confuses training and development. Emerging (1-2): Generic answer. (9 marks.)
